content: Routine management of chylothorax in neonates typically involves either conservative measures or surgical interventions. Octreotide, a synthetic analogue of somatostatin, has been employed in cases of refractory chylothorax that do not respond to conservative treatment. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of octreotide in treating neonatal chylothorax. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE databases up to March 7, 2010. Additionally, reference lists of identified studies and abstracts from Pediatric Academic Societies meetings (2002–2009) published in Pediatric Research were reviewed. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The inclusion criteria specified randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving neonates, either term or preterm, with congenital or acquired chylothorax. Studies were eligible regardless of the dose, duration, or route of octreotide administration. Data collection was planned to focus on primary outcomes such as the volume of fluid drainage, respiratory support requirements, and mortality, as well as secondary outcomes like adverse effects. Statistical analyses were to be performed using mean difference, relative risk, and risk difference with 95% confidence intervals. However, no randomized controlled trials were identified during the search. Instead, 19 case reports involving 20 neonates treated with octreotide (administered either subcutaneously or intravenously) were found. Among these, 14 case reports documented successful resolution of chylothorax, four reported treatment failure, and one described equivocal results. The timing of treatment initiation, dosing regimens, duration, and frequency of administration varied significantly across cases. Reported adverse effects included gastrointestinal intolerance, clinical signs suggestive of necrotizing enterocolitis, and transient hypothyroidism. Based on the evidence reviewed, no definitive clinical recommendations can be made regarding the use of octreotide for neonatal chylothorax. The authors emphasize the need for a prospective registry of chylothorax cases and a subsequent multicenter randomized controlled trial to rigorously evaluate the safety and efficacy of octreotide in this context.
